description: In the era of nugatory content, media and games, it is crucial that there are programmes being designed for children to learn, to unlock their curiosity and to set them on the path to become humanity's next leaders. Because of our desire to raise the next generation of scientists, researchers and industry specialists me and my friends have decided to set on to create a game that not only is engaging and entertaining but also plants the seeds for a life full of scientific curiosity.
summary:
"What is it like to work at NASA?" Many of us have asked ourselves that question, and we developed a (simplified) answer to that. Our project has the goal of teaching children about NASA, from the other side of the learning experience, NASA's one.

"Directive Zero" more than a game, is an experience. The game starts when the player becomes the doctor in charge of a highly classified (and with unlimited budget) directive, that is divided in 3 Chapters where the player constructs missions in order to explore the moon, mars and outer space. 

Through our "Learn by doing" dynamic, we strive to immerse the player in the real-life challenges that the cutting-edge researchers of our generation are faced with and teach the player about the wonders that the minds of NASA scientists are capable of achieving. 

After finishing each mission, the player can see the real-life footage of their mission launching, further immersing the player and showing that the almost sci-fi looking missions NASA develops are actually possible.

In the current mediatic context of nugatory content, our game strives to stray away the minds of children from this type of content and lead them to the world outside of ours. By teaching them interactively the scientific, technological and humanitarian breakthroughs of NASA, we hope to raise the next generation of young scientist that will lead real-life missions, like the ones that inspired us in this challenge.
details:
The game starts by personalizing the experience and how the player is addressed throughout the game. This first line personalization is what characterizes the rest of the game.

While there is a lot of information as to what NASA does and how do they do it, we have managed to package it in a way that catches the eye of children who are hooked up to nugatory content - our target group. In the 13 missions the player learns about the different parts and goals that NASA missions have and experiences first-hand, the assembly process of real-life NASA missions. The whole experience concludes almost theatrically with real-life footage of the rocket launches of these missions. We have essentially let the player answer their own questions about NASA missions.

To bring our project to life we have used the game developing engine "Unity" which helped us visualize our project as we were building it. Moreover, within this engine there are C# scripts which are the sentences that the elements of our game speak. For the development of the game, we used both 2D and 3D elements that were taken directly either from NASA Images or the NASA 3D archive. Finally using the Build Profile for Android we made the APK file that is available in our Google Drive Repository along with the project Demo.

More than a game our project takes the experience an thrill of being a NASA scientist and packages it in a way that is engaging for even toddlers. Thats what sets us apart, we have not created not a mere slideshow presenting NASA misions, we took the information and thought like a child, for a child.

(A little easter egg of our game is that when a player doesn't choose a name, the placeholder last name is Hamilton, honoring the late NASA Computer Scientist)
